messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Weber was 49, a married European American city council member who had built a public life in which he was expected to shake hands, stand close to constituents, and remain composed under scrutiny. Long before he sought help, he had started arranging his days around the wariness he felt in his own body. He kept the television or radio on at home far more than his wife preferred, filling the house with loud sound so there would be less room for his thoughts. If he found himself alone with silence, he became preoccupied with checking whether he was “still in control,” watching for any sign that he was going crazy. He also found any physical contact difficult; even a casual touch on the arm or back from a colleague, neighbor, or volunteer could make him jerk away before he had time to think.

Daniel traced all of this back to combat service years earlier, when he had been in a situation that taught him, in a matter of moments, that he could not rely on his surroundings or even on his own body to stay steady. He did not describe the event in a neat sequence. When he tried, he would lose the thread and stop mid-sentence, frustrated and embarrassed by how much of it felt out of reach. What he could say was that the memory came to him in fragments: pieces of terrain, flashes of movement, a sense of noise and urgency, and then blank stretches where the rest should have been. That missing quality was part of what unsettled him most. He knew something terrible had happened, but the memory never settled into a complete picture. Instead, it arrived as broken parts that did not fit together.

When he did remember, the terror was immediate and bodily. He would not simply think about it; he would feel himself back there, with the same sharp fear he had felt at the time. Those moments could be triggered by ordinary life in unexpected ways. A hand landing on his shoulder from behind in a crowded city hall corridor could make his whole body lock up. A passing comment from a staff member that “you’re safe now” did little to reassure him, because he had come to believe that safety could not be trusted just because someone said so. Even in his own office, where he was known and respected, he watched doors, sounds, and people constantly, as if danger could return without warning. He felt that he had to stay on guard all the time, and that state of readiness had become part of his daily rhythm.

At night, the same sense of alertness followed him into bed. He had trouble falling asleep, and when sleep did come, he woke easily and often stayed awake thinking about whether he had missed something. The quiet hours were especially difficult because they left him alone with the feeling that his body was still responding as if he were in danger even when nothing around him was threatening. He described this as his body becoming an enemy of sorts, reacting before he could reason with it, making him tense, jumpy, and unable to settle. The more this happened, the more convinced he became that the world itself was dangerous, not in some abstract way but in the practical sense that harm could appear suddenly and without warning.

Over time, Daniel’s avoidance became organized around preventing those moments of alarm. He kept conversations shorter when they might drift toward the war, and when others tried to reassure him, he found himself inwardly rejecting their words. He avoided situations in which people might touch him unexpectedly, including the handshakes and back pats that were routine in his political work. At home, his wife learned to announce herself before coming close, and even then he sometimes stiffened. He did not want to be treated as fragile, yet he had come to live in a way that made ordinary contact feel risky. His wife noticed how often he sat with the television turned up, how he checked himself for signs of panic, and how tired he seemed from sleeping poorly and remaining watchful.

By the time he came for help, it was because the effort of maintaining that guarded life had become too hard to hide. He was still functioning publicly, but it took more energy than he could sustain, and he was increasingly afraid of what it meant that his body reacted so strongly to harmless contact and his memories still carried the same terror years later. What brought him in was not a single crisis so much as the growing realization that he could no longer trust his own sense of safety. He wanted relief from the constant vigilance, but he was also afraid that if he let his guard down, something terrible would catch him unprepared again.
